title: He Mocked Barnett Newman's Joke While Newman Was Still Finishing It
standfirst: In 1968 Frank Bowling stencilled a map of the country that had just become independent into a parody of Barnett Newman, demoting his rival's name to a schoolyard nickname. Three years later, writing about what his own red and green stripes did not mean, he took the joke a step further.

sections.heading: A Joke Aimed at an Unfinished Target
sections.body: Barnett Newman's *Who's Afraid of Red, Yellow and Blue* [took its title](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Who%27s_Afraid_of_Red,_Yellow_and_Blue) from Edward Albee's 1962 play, itself a nod to the old Disney tune about the big bad wolf. Newman painted the first canvas in 1966 and two more, II and III, the year after; the fourth and last of the series wasn't finished until 1969 or 1970. Frank Bowling made *Who's Afraid of Barney Newman* in 1968 — squarely inside that gap. Newman was still working through his own joke when Bowling handed it back to him, trading the older painter's given name for the diminutive a schoolyard uses on someone it doesn't respect.

sections.heading: The Technique Came From a Paint Chemist, Not a Painter
sections.body: Bowling had [arrived in New York in 1966](https://frankbowling.com/biography/), drawn into its studios and openings by an older generation that included Larry Rivers. But the method behind this canvas came from elsewhere: he grew friendly with [Leonard Bocour](https://www.sfmoma.org/read/mapping-a-life-in-paint-an-interview-with-frank-bowling/), one of the chemists who had pioneered acrylic paint, and started working with materials nobody had taught him at the Royal College of Art — spray paint borrowed from graffiti writers, fluorescent and pearlescent pigment, gel medium, ammonia, turpentine, beeswax. The shapes that became his map paintings weren't planned as a political programme. Bowling later traced them to the sun moving across the windows of the Chelsea Hotel while he worked with silkscreen, throwing shadows he began to follow — Guyana, South America, Africa came out of that. The result, [236 by 129.5 centimetres](https://frankbowling.com/artworks/3339-frank-bowling-who-s-afraid-of-barney-newman-1968/) of acrylic, is closer to soaked than brushed.

sections.heading: One Set of Colours, Three Incompatible Explanations
sections.body: The painting sets a yellow stripe — Newman's own "zip" — between a block of red and a block of green, with an outline of South America stencilled along the seam. Guyana had become [independent of Britain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guyana) on 26 May 1966, two years before Bowling painted this, and its new flag used exactly that red, gold and green: officially, gold for mineral wealth, green for agriculture and forests, red for ["zeal and dynamism."](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flag_of_Guyana) Bowling never said the stripes were the flag. Three years later, in an essay titled "It's Not Enough to Say Black Is Beautiful," he [went further](https://www.thenation.com/article/culture/frank-bowling-painter-profile/) and denied the colours carried any racial charge at all: "we have not been able to detect in any kind of universal sense The Black Experience wedged-up in the flat bed between red and green: between say a red stripe and a green stripe."

sections.heading: A Show Built to Make the Same Point Twice
sections.body: In late 1969, a year after finishing this canvas, Bowling organised an exhibition called ["5+1"](https://www.mfa.org/beyond-the-gallery/frank-bowling-and-5-1) at Stony Brook University, hanging his own work alongside Melvin Edwards, Daniel LaRue Johnson, Al Loving, Jack Whitten and William T. Williams — five Black American artists working in abstraction, none of it figurative, none of it protest art. Bowling said the show was meant to "once and for all put a stop" to exhibitions that grouped Black artists by race rather than by what the work actually did. He held the [contributing-editor's chair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Bowling) at Arts Magazine through 1972, using it to argue, essay after essay, against the exact reading his own stripes kept attracting.

sections.heading: The Series He Borrowed the Joke From Ended Under a Knife
sections.body: Newman's own Who's Afraid of Red, Yellow and Blue didn't stay a private joke between two painters. In 1986 a man named Gerard Jan van Bladeren [attacked the third canvas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Who%27s_Afraid_of_Red,_Yellow_and_Blue) with a knife at the Stedelijk Museum in Amsterdam, apparently because he could find nothing in it worth reading. The restoration that followed was its own kind of violence: the restorer repainted the damaged section with a roller, over-varnished the whole canvas, then [sued the museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Who%27s_Afraid_of_Red,_Yellow_and_Blue) for $125 million when critics objected. A court didn't force the full report into the open until 2013; it confirmed what the critics had said all along. Bowling's canvas, carrying a title that names that same series, has had a quieter life. It hangs now in [Tate Britain](https://www.tate.org.uk/art/artworks/bowling-whos-afraid-of-barney-newman-t12244), which gave him his first full retrospective in 2019.
